extracted.intended_audience: IP attorneys, patent owners/parties, and counsel handling PTAB appeals and Rule 90 extension requests
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating or preparing a request to extend the time to file a notice of appeal of a PTAB decision under 37 C.F.R. § 90.3(c)(1)(ii) based on excusable neglect, applying the Federal Courts/Pioneer framework. Covers what factual showings and factors the Director (via the Solicitor) will consider in deciding such extension requests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jurisdictional deadline to seek judicial review
rubrics_metrics.description: Under 37 C.F.R. § 90.3(a)(1), judicial review of a Board decision must be sought within sixty-three (63) days of the Board decision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A Notice of Appeal must be filed with the Director within 63 days of the Board decision; parties often also file a copy with the Federal Circuit. Calculate the 63-day deadline from the Board decision date (example: Board decision May 9, 2023 → deadline July 11, 2023).

rubrics_metrics.name: Authority for time extensions under Rule 90.3(c)(1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rule 90.3(c)(1) allows parties extra time to file a notice of appeal in the Federal Circuit under two circumstances: (i) Director may extend time for a filing requested before expiration for good cause (90.3(c)(1)(i)); (ii) Director may extend time for a filing requested after expiration due to excusable neglect (90.3(c)(1)(ii)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The present request, filed after the filing period expired, falls under the excusable neglect provision (90.3(c)(1)(ii)). Authority to decide such requests has been delegated to the Solicitor (see MPEP § 1002.02(k)(3)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard applied for 'excusable neglect'
rubrics_metrics.description: The USPTO applies the standard used by the Federal Courts (Pioneer Inv. Servs. Co. v. Brunswick Assocs. Ltd. P'ship, 507 U.S. 380 (1993)) in determining whether failure to act was the result of excusable neglect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Excusable neglect is an equitable, fact-specific inquiry taking account of all relevant circumstances surrounding the omission. It may encompass negligence but is not strictly limited to circumstances beyond the movant's control. Reliance on acts/omissions of the party's chosen counsel is permissible when relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pioneer factors for excusable neglect
rubrics_metrics.description: The generally considered factors are: (1) danger of prejudice to another party; (2) length of the delay and its potential impact on judicial proceedings; (3) reason for the delay, including whether it was within the reasonable control of the movant; and (4) whether the movant acted in good faith.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The third factor (reason for the delay) is generally viewed as the most important, although it does not control the inquiry. All factors should be weighed together in an equitable analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of counsel's acts and omissions
rubrics_metrics.description: In determining excusable neglect, it is proper to rely on the acts and omissions of a party's chosen counsel where relevant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although inadvertence, ignorance of the rules, or mistakes construing the rules do not usually constitute excusable neglect, negligence (including carelessness by counsel) can be excusable depending on the circumstances and the Pioneer factors. Case citations (e.g., Pioneer; Cheney v. Anchor Glass Container Corp.) illustrate contexts where negligence was found excusable given lack of prejudice and bad faith.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity of detailed factual explanation for delay (third factor)
rubrics_metrics.description: A request must provide a sufficiently detailed explanation of why the filing was delayed, including whether the delay was within the movant's reasonable control.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relevant factual detail includes who attended meetings about appealability, the outcome of such meetings, who at the client had authority to decide to appeal, to whom instructions were communicated, when/how instructions were transmitted and memorialized, which firm was instructed to file, why that firm did not receive instructions or did not monitor the docket, the role and obligations of counsel of record (e.g., to monitor deadlines), whether any docketing systems existed, and how the movant became aware of the missed deadline. Failure to provide such specifics weighs heavily against finding excusable neglect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment of prejudice and impact (first and second factors)
rubrics_metrics.description: The absence of evidence showing prejudice to another party and no meaningful delay or negative impact on judicial or administrative proceedings weighs in favor of granting the extension.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrate no prejudice and no meaningful impact on ongoing proceedings to strengthen the request. The length of the delay and its practical consequences are relevant and should be addressed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good faith (fourth factor)
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence that the movant acted in good faith (no bad faith) supports a finding of excusable neglect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prompt action upon discovery of the error (e.g., immediate instruction to file notice of appeal upon learning of missed deadline) and lack of manipulative behavior are relevant. The record should show that delay was not caused by bad faith.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typical outcomes and procedural relief
rubrics_metrics.description: Requests under § 90.3(c)(1)(ii) may be denied without prejudice or granted; denial may be without prejudice to filing another request within a specified short period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example outcome here: request denied without prejudice but with leave to file another request within seven calendar days. Concurrent or subsequent filing of a late notice of appeal with the Director and docketing at the Federal Circuit do not foreclose the Director's authority to decide the Rule 90 request.
